identity_notes: D-ribose evidence splits cleanly by indication. In McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease type V), two Cochrane systematic reviews (PMID 21154353, updated as 25391139) explicitly report NO benefit from D-ribose and, in the updated review, note adverse effects (diarrhoea, hypoglycemia-like symptoms) — this is the strongest and most negative evidence in the set. In athletic/exercise performance (anaerobic capacity, recovery, DOMS), results are mixed-to-null in the largest, cleanest single-agent trials (12660407, 16521849, 18178380) with occasional subgroup-specific positive findings (29296106: benefit only in lower-fitness subjects; 32778175: DOMS reduction). In cardiovascular/heart-failure indications, D-ribose is almost always tested as one component of a MULTI-INGREDIENT combination product (with ubiquinol, creatine, CoQ10, vitamin E, vitamin B1/B6, or nicotinamide) rather than alone — the single positive-leaning factorial RCT with a D-ribose-alone arm (35644694, n=216, HFpEF) reports pooled 'ubiquinol and/or d-ribose' results without isolating the D-ribose-alone arm's effect in the abstract, so the isolated-ribose effect size cannot be confirmed from this scope. Two IV/infusion route studies (8880031, 19200398, both nuclear cardiology stress-imaging contexts) were rejected as not_this_route since the label material is an oral supplement. A perioperative surgical protocol (21693564) used D-ribose in an ambiguous, likely non-oral route and is flagged for reviewer attention. Several off-topic false-positive retrievals occurred from keyword overlap with unrelated chemistry (antisense-oligonucleotide '2'-methoxyethyl-D-ribose' backbones, tuberculosis drug trials, Ribose-5-phosphate isomerase enzymology, Autoinducer-2 bacterial signaling molecule) — none of these concern the dietary supplement D-ribose.
